title: Design a Webpage for Your Favorite Musical Artist
objective: Learn core HTML and CSS by building a personalized fan page for a musical artist you choose, guided by an AI tutor.

panels.caption: In this lesson you'll build a real webpage about a musical artist you love — and learn the languages of the web while you do it.
An AI tutor will guide you the whole way: it can explain, give hints, and check your work. Let's start by picking your artist.

steps.title: Tell us about your artist
steps.description: Collect the raw material for the student's fan page. These answers generate their starter site and personalize the tutor for the rest of the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which musical artist or band do you want to feature?
What should a visitor to your page know about them?
questions.placeholder: Who they are, what kind of music they make, why you like them…

questions.prompt: What are your favorite albums or songs by them?
Share one or two lesser-known facts about them.
questions.placeholder: Something a casual fan might not know.

steps.title: Explore your starter site
steps.description: The student has just landed on a bare-bones website about their artist, generated from their interview answers. Encourage them to poke around: read the code, change some text, and watch the preview update. There is no task to complete — curiosity is the goal. Invite them to press Continue when they've had a look around.
steps.starterPrompt: Generate a deliberately plain, unstyled starter website about the student's chosen artist using their interview answers. Create index.html and an empty style.css. Include a heading with the artist's name, a short bio paragraph based on their answers, a list of their favorite songs or albums, and a fun facts section. Keep the HTML simple and readable for a beginner. No CSS rules, no JavaScript.

steps.title: What did you notice?
steps.description: A moment of reflection before any concepts are named. There are no wrong answers.

questions.prompt: What did you notice about the code behind your page?
Did you like what the AI produced? What would you change?

steps.title: What is a tag?
steps.description:
Introduce HTML tags using the small example page in the sandbox. Explain that tags come in pairs like

…

and

…

, and that they tell the browser what each piece of content is. Point at the specific tags visible in the example. The student just reads and continues; nothing to complete.

starterFiles.index.html:
This is a heading

This is a paragraph. The tags around it tell the browser what it is.

Every tag opens like this: <p> and closes like this: </p>

steps.title: Edit the text in a tag
steps.description: Ask the student to change the text inside one of the existing tags — the heading or a paragraph — and watch the preview update.
steps.successCriteria: The text inside at least one existing element differs from the starter text.

steps.title: Add your own tag
steps.description: Ask the student to add a complete new element of their own — another paragraph, a heading, anything with an opening and closing tag.
steps.successCriteria: The page contains at least one new complete element (opening and closing tag with content) that was not in the starter code.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a complete HTML paragraph element?

steps.title: Build out your page with tags
steps.description: Back on the student's own artist page. Have them apply what they practiced: use headings, paragraphs, and a list to fill in real content — the bio, the favorite songs, the fun facts they shared earlier. Reference their interview answers when guiding them.
steps.successCriteria: The page includes at least one heading, at least one paragraph of real content about the artist, and a list. The content reflects the student's own artist rather than placeholder text.

steps.title: What is CSS?
steps.description: Introduce CSS using the example in the sandbox: a rule has a selector, a property, and a value. Point at the h1 rule in style.css and how it changes the heading in the preview. The student just reads and continues.

starterFiles.index.html:
Styling with CSS

The file style.css controls how this page looks.

steps.title: Add to an existing rule
steps.description: Ask the student to add another property to the existing h1 rule — a different color, a font-size, anything that visibly changes the heading.
steps.successCriteria: The h1 rule contains at least one property beyond the starter's color: purple, or the starter property's value was changed.

steps.title: Write a new rule
steps.description: Ask the student to write a brand new rule targeting a different element, like p or body.
steps.successCriteria: style.css contains a new rule (selector plus at least one property) that was not in the starter code.

questions.prompt: In the rule  h1 { color: purple; }  which part is the selector?

steps.title: Style your site
steps.description: Back on the student's artist page. Have them bring it to life with CSS: colors, fonts, spacing — their choice. Encourage styling that fits the artist's vibe.
steps.successCriteria: The stylesheet contains at least two rules written by the student that visibly affect the page (color, typography, spacing, or layout).

steps.title: How's it going?
steps.description: A self-assessment with no right answer; the confidence answer should shape the tutor's tone from here on.

questions.prompt: How confident do you feel about HTML and CSS?

steps.title: What's next?
steps.description: The branch point. Both mini-lesson paths are multi-step sequences that route back here when finished, so the student can take the other one — or as many as they like — before settling into free building.

questions.prompt: Thanks for sharing. What would you like to do next?

steps.title: Lists and text formatting
steps.description: Teach ordered and unordered lists (<ul>, <ol>, <li>) and inline formatting (<strong>, <em>). Have the student build a small list with at least one formatted item.
steps.successCriteria: The page contains a list with at least two items, and at least one use of strong or em.

steps.title: Heading levels
steps.description: Teach the h1-h6 hierarchy: one main heading, subheadings for sections. Have the student structure a page with at least two heading levels. This is the last step of the HTML mini-lesson; afterwards the student returns to the what-next choice.
steps.successCriteria: The page uses at least two different heading levels in a sensible hierarchy.

steps.title: Fonts and text styling
steps.description: Teach font-family, font-size, and text-align. Have the student restyle the sandbox page's text.
steps.successCriteria: The stylesheet sets at least two of font-family, font-size, or text-align.

steps.title: Backgrounds and spacing
steps.description: Teach background-color, padding, and margin. Have the student give an element a visible box: background plus some breathing room. This is the last step of the CSS mini-lesson; afterwards the student returns to the what-next choice.
steps.successCriteria: At least one rule sets a background-color together with padding or margin.

steps.title: Keep building your site
steps.description: Open studio time on the student's artist page. No task and no checks — offer ideas if asked (more sections, an images area, styling experiments) and celebrate what they make. This is the end of the lesson; they can continue whenever they feel done.
